clips.text_en_c1: Were you compelled to commit your entire portfolio to a single asset for the coming decade, the choice between Bitcoin and gold presents a dilemma that few investors can settle with any confidence. An anonymous poster on 4chan's /biz/ board posed precisely this question to the community, prompting a thread that has since fractured into two entrenched camps: gold bugs who dismiss cryptocurrency as an elaborate speculative bubble, and Bitcoin maximalists who regard the metal as a relic of an obsolete financial era.
clips.text_en_c2: An anonymous poster on /biz/ posed what he framed as a generational dilemma: given a ten-year horizon and the necessity of a single long-only position, which asset merits the conviction—Bitcoin or gold? Predictably, the thread bifurcated into two entrenched camps. The maximalists contend that no quantity of fiat erosion or regulatory pressure can erode Bitcoin's programmed scarcity, whereas the goldbugs invoke millennia of monetary precedent to argue that Bitcoin remains an untested, volatile experiment. Both factions, however, converge on a single assertion—that their chosen instrument constitutes the sole authentic repository of value amid systemic debasement. The OP, presently bleeding capital at a proprietary trading firm, confesses he harbours ambitions for both yet lacks the liquidity to indulge either fully, while remaining exasperated by Bitcoin's mercurial swings and dismissive of bullion as dormant capital.

clips.text_en_b2: You watch Bitcoin sit completely flat for weeks on end and ignore it entirely. Then it suddenly pumps 15 percent and everyone rushes in, chasing the move after it has already happened. Anons in the thread complain bitterly that they keep buying at the top instead of loading up during the boring sideways action, since getting in late tends to destroy you.
clips.text_en_c1: The psychology underpinning retail crypto trading is, frankly, something to behold in its predictability. One observes Bitcoin consolidate within a narrow band for weeks on end, a period during which retail interest entirely evaporates, and the moment a fifteen percent vertical move materialises, every lagging participant scrambles to chase the breakout. The thread captures this recurring phenomenon with characteristic candour, as multiple anonymous contributors lament the brutal lesson they have absorbed from chasing momentum entries on CFDs. The sentiment among seasoned participants is unambiguous: while the flat, directionless days feel excruciatingly tedious, that is precisely when capital ought to be deployed, since entries following a fifteen percent surge more often…
clips.text_en_c2: There is a peculiar pathology afflicting retail participants that manifests whenever Bitcoin enters a consolidation phase: while price action stagnates over several weeks, ostensibly generating no actionable signal whatsoever, the moment a 15% vertical ascent materialises, the very same cohort that studiously ignored the preceding quiescence develops an overwhelming compulsion to chase the move. Anons in the thread diagnose this phenomenon as a textbook instance of recency bias compounded by FOMO dynamics, lamenting that capital is invariably deployed at structurally suboptimal moments. The poster himself concedes he learned this lesson the hard way via a CFD position, observing that discipline during the boring, eventless accumulation phase would have been vastly more lucrative than any reactive entry he subsequently attempted.

clips.text_en_c1: What course of action ought one to pursue were one to develop a credible suspicion that OpenAI had appropriated one's research and programs in order to engineer significant breakthroughs? The thread documents the case of researcher Tristan Buckmaster, who, having spent considerable effort developing his methodology using Codex and Claude, was subsequently struck by the remarkable resemblance between his own framework and what OpenAI marketed as their GPT-6 Astra solution. The implication circulating among contributors is that frontier labs may be training their models upon work produced by the very researchers who turn to those same tools for assistance, an arrangement that raises rather uncomfortable questions about consent and intellectual…
clips.text_en_c2: Within the thread, contributors grapple with an increasingly disquieting epistemic question: what ought one to do should credible evidence emerge that OpenAI has appropriated one's proprietary research and bespoke programs to engineer subsequent breakthroughs? The discussion foregrounds the case of Tristan Buckmaster, a researcher who observed that OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra solution bore a striking structural resemblance to work he had independently cultivated using Codex and Claude. Whether this constitutes deliberate appropriation or convergent methodological evolution remains contested, yet the broader concern animating the discussion is whether established professionals—surveyors, analysts, credentialed specialists still navigating their own examinations—are destined to witness their livelihoods methodically automated, rendered obsolescent by systems trained upon the very expertise they spent decades refining.

clips.text_en_b2: A new OECD PISA study tested roughly 760,000 students across 91 countries, and the global results in maths and reading comprehension are falling sharply, except in China. The top tier in maths, level 5, starts at 607, yet the average Chinese student scores 612. That means ordinary Chinese pupils hit what counts as elite performance almost anywhere else.
clips.text_en_c1: The latest OECD PISA assessment, which evaluated roughly 760,000 students spanning 91 countries, has delivered results that ought to give Western educators considerable pause. Whereas global performance in both mathematical literacy and reading comprehension continues its precipitous decline, China has once again emerged as a conspicuous outlier, with the average Chinese student scoring 612 in mathematics. To contextualise what that figure represents, level 5 competence, the threshold beyond which performance is classified as elite, commences at 607, meaning an ordinary Chinese pupil attains what other nations would consider the mark of an exceptional one.
clips.text_en_c2: The latest OECD PISA assessment, encompassing some 760,000 students across 91 participating nations, delivers what can only be described as a grim verdict on global educational standards—mathematical and reading comprehension scores have collectively cratered almost everywhere. China, however, emerges as the conspicuous and almost implausible outlier in this landscape of institutional regression. The benchmark for elite mathematical attainment, level five, commences at a threshold of 607; the average Chinese pupil, by contrast, registers 612, thereby rendering ordinary competency in that jurisdiction indistinguishable from the highest tier achieved virtually anywhere else. Whether this reflects genuine pedagogical ascendancy or the relentless machinery of examination culture remains a matter of vigorous contestation, though Hong Kong's notoriously exacting parentage surely greets such figures with quiet satisfaction.

clips.text_en_c1: News that Blizzard employees have ratified what is being characterised as a landmark union contract has reverberated throughout the gaming community, particularly given the broader industrial backdrop of mass layoffs and the creeping encroachment of artificial intelligence across development pipelines. The contract, which trade observers suggest could establish a meaningful precedent for the entire games industry, reportedly contains explicit provisions safeguarding workers against AI replacement, a stipulation that anons have greeted with caustic humour. The irony, as several contributors are eager to point out, is delicious: a studio long associated with some of the industry's most contentious labour practices has, quite unexpectedly, positioned itself at the vanguard of worker protections.
clips.text_en_c2: News that Blizzard's workforce has ratified what observers are heralding as a landmark union contract—one that establishes a precedential benchmark for the broader game development industry—has provoked responses oscillating between incredulity and guarded optimism. Anons, predictably, juxtapose this development against the spectre of AI displacement, noting that whilst competitive esports remain entirely tangential to their concerns, the labour movement itself resembles reportage from an alternate universe where organised workforces and corporate behemoths negotiate in good faith. The original coverage, courtesy of GameSpot, details provisions reportedly affording enhanced job security specifically against automation-related redundancies, leading contributors to declare—with characteristic irony—that the once-mighty Blizzard has, at last on this singular matter, reacquired some semblance of its former relevance.

clips.text_en_b1: Is there anything more retarded than the calories in calories out dogma? If you are getting fatter, of course you are storing more calories. But that does not tell you WHY. It is like asking why Elon Musk is so rich and answering because he took in more money than he spent. The thread says this is a useless tautology.
clips.source_hint: /fit/ thread ranting about CICO fitness dogma
clips.text_en_b2: Is there anything more idiotic than the calories in calories out dogma? If you are piling on weight, of course you are storing more calories than you burn. But that tells you absolutely nothing about the underlying reasons. It is a bit like asking why Elon Musk is so wealthy and answering that he earns more than he spends, which is basically a useless tautology.
clips.text_en_c1: There exists a creed within fitness circles, the so-called calories in, calories out doctrine, which is bandied about with such zealous conviction that any attempt at critical examination is typically met with reflexive hostility. Yet the framework, stripped of its pseudo-scientific veneer, reduces to a sterile tautology of staggering uselessness, since observing that a person gaining weight must necessarily be storing additional energy merely restates the phenomenon without illuminating its underlying causation. It is precisely analogous to responding to the question of how Elon Musk amassed his fortune with the observation that his revenues exceeded his expenditures, a technically accurate yet profoundly vacuous non-answer that the thread rightly lampoons.
clips.text_en_c2: There is perhaps no doctrine more analytically bankrupt than the catechism known as calories in, calories out, which its critics rightly identify as a vacuous tautology masquerading as nutritional science. Confronted with an individual demonstrably gaining adipose tissue, one might as well ask why Elon Musk amasses fortunes and receive the reply that his revenues exceeded his expenditures—technically accurate, entirely vacuous, and functionally useless as either explanation or prescription. The thread's contributors eviscerate this framework with evident relish, arguing that the CICO paradigm deliberately elides the constellation of hormonal, metabolic, psychological, and environmental determinants that actually govern energy partition. Any overweight reader witnessing this deconstruction is earnestly entreated to tag the original poster, lest such culinary-philosophical heresy propagate unchallenged.
